messages.author: 1fe638ac9008754d
messages.subject: Issues with n divergent that I can't seem to improve
parts:
Hi,

I have been having issues with a meta-analysis model (of insect captures over time, after an initial release), resulting in nDivergent=1 across much of my sample. A simplified model for a particular study is of the form shown below. When I run the stan model using: 

fit <- stan(file='NBGompertzStanGroup.stan',
            data=list(Y=c(12, 8, 7, 2, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0),numReleased=1191),
            chains=1,iter=2000,
            seed=1)

I get 1287 divergent iterations. I have tried increasing adapt_delta, but this doesn't appear to improve things. I have also used a similar model (discrete Weibull), as well as tried a poisson likelihood, (I attach all three models - the original shown below is 'NBGompertzStanGroup), but all suffer the same fate. Does anyone have any idea how I can rectify this issue?

data {
  int numReleased; ## Number of insects released
  int Y[11]; ## Number collected
  } 
  
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> psi;
  real<lower=0> beta;
  real<lower=0> alpha;
  real<lower=0> kappa;
} 

model {
  real lambda[11];
  for (t in 1:11){
    lambda[t]<- numReleased*psi*exp(-alpha*(exp(beta*t)-1)/beta);
Y[t] ~ neg_binomial_2(lambda[t]+1e-05,kappa);
  }
  psi ~ uniform(0,1); ## Probability of recapture
  alpha ~ normal(0,5); ## Parameter 1 of Gompertz mortality
  beta ~ normal(0,5); ## Parameter 2 of Gompertz mortality
  kappa ~ uniform(0,100); ## Dispersion parameter of NB
}

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Issues with n divergent that I can't seem to improve
parts:
I think lambda is OK as is, but kappa isn't --- it
should have upper=100 to match this:

> real<lower=0> kappa;
> kappa ~ uniform(0,100); ## Dispersion parameter of NB

I don't understand why the magic number 1e-5 is there (nor
do I understand the "0" in "1e-05" --- I didn't even think it
was legal to start a number with "0"):
> Y[t] ~ neg_binomial_2(lambda[t]+1e-05,kappa);

I'd think the bigger issue would be with kappa being near zero.
So I think you need to go into the model and instrument with print()
statements to see where things are diverging. Or define generated
quantities like

> numReleased*psi*exp(-alpha*(exp(beta*t)-1)/beta)

to see what's happening to the values.

The inner plus outer exponential form is tricky, because the psi,
alpha, and beta are going to wind up highly correlated in the
posterior.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Issues with n divergent that I can't seem to improve
parts:
What I was trying to convey is that the model should have
support for all parameter values satisfying the declared constraints.

I believe in this case, Andrew's recommending an overdispersion variable only
constrained to be positive

real<lower=0> kappa;

But if this is all you did, you'd get an improper uniform, so to
satisfy the "no uniform priors!" dictum, you need a prior

kappa ~ ...;

But I don't know which one Andrew would suggest for overdispersion in
neg_binomial_2. Andrew, your Wiki awaits:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

And just to clarify, Andrew, should we get rid of all uniform priors in
the manual, even the unconstrained ones, or is it just the interval constraint
you object to? That is, should we not have regressions with
improper uniform priors on coefficients and scale as examples?

As is, we have quite a few models in our examples repo that use these
uniform priors constrained to an interval. We can prioritize updating
those if we can deprioritize something else. Or find a volunteer willing
to go through them.

- Bob

parts:
Hello all,

Thank you for your suggestions. 

Whilst your points generally focus on the dispersion parameter, I would say that even for the Poisson model I get the same results (here I have included the perhaps simpler Weibull mortality) below. I also attach a scatter plot of samples from the posterior (although to be clear here, since I have divergent iterations, it isn't really the posterior, but this result comes up from simulations of fake data as well, where there are no divergent iterations), and we see that beta and mu are highly correlated. This makes intuitive sense, since either you can explain the data by having a high mortality and low age effects, or vice versa. So it is difficult to identify beta. 

However, I don't understand how to prevent this early termination of NUTS nonetheless. I think it's to do with the sensitivity of the system to changes in beta, but am not sure.

Any ideas?

Best,

Ben

data {
  int numReleased; ## Number of insects released
  int Y[11]; ## Number collected
  } 
  
parameters {
  real<lower=0,upper=1> psi;

real<lower=1> beta;
  real<lower=0,upper=1> mu;

} 

model {
  real lambda[11];
  for (t in 1:11){

lambda[t]<- numReleased*psi*((1-mu)^(t))^beta;
Y[t] ~ poisson(lambda[t]);

}
  psi ~ uniform(0,1); ## Probability of recapture

mu ~ uniform(0,1); ## Parameter 1 of weibull
  beta ~ uniform(1,5); ## Parameter 1 of weibull
}

I will

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Issues with n divergent that I can't seem to improve
parts:
Unlike BUGS or JAGS, Stan requires any parameter value that meets the
constraint, here

> real<lower=1> beta;

to have support in the model,
> beta ~ uniform(1,5); ## Parameter 1 of weibull

which fails here. The value beta can be > 5 according
to the constraint, but that has no support in the model. If you
get near that boundary you'll terminate early.

To save Andrew the trouble, let me say that he doesn't
recommend uniform priors. We're working on fixing the examples
we distributed earlier that are coded like this.

- Bob

I also attach a scatter plot of samples from the posterior (although to be clear here, since I have divergent iterations, it isn't really the posterior, but this result comes up from simulations of fake data as well, where there are no divergent iterations), and we see that beta and mu are highly correlated. This makes intuitive sense, since either you can explain the data by having a high mortality and low age effects, or vice versa. So it is difficult to identify beta.
>
> However, I don't understand how to prevent this early termination of NUTS nonetheless. I think it's to do with the sensitivity of the system to changes in beta, but am not sure.
>
> Any ideas?
>
> Best,
>
> Ben

> }

> }
> psi ~ uniform(0,1); ## Probability of recapture

> beta ~ uniform(1,5); ## Parameter 1 of weibull
> }

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: On uniform priors
parts:
Hi, yes, I agree with Bob that if you really have a constrained prior on a parameter, it makes sense to define it on a constrained space. But I really don’t like these uniform(0,A) priors. If you want to constrain a parameter to be less than 100, say, it’s my guess that you really think your parameter is less than 10, and maybe something like an exponential(.1) prior would do the job.

Unconstrained uniforms (i.e., in Stan, not putting in a prior at all) are another story. They’re wrong too, of course, but they’re not pretending to be anything they’re not. If you don’t put in a prior, it’s understood that you are ready to put in a real prior later, if necessary.
